newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space probe heads for dark asteroid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space probe heads for dark asteroid.

text.p: A small NASA space probe is heading for a close encounter with a space rock so black one scientist calls it a "stealth asteroid," scientists said on Monday.

The NEAR spacecraft, built for the U.S. space agency by the Johns Hopkins University, is to speed past the asteroid Mathilde on Friday on its way to a rendezvous with the asteroid Eros in January 1999.
"This is bonus science," said Robert Farquhar, the Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous mission director. "We didn't really plan for this fly-by, it just happened fortuitously."
It will be the first time a space probe from earth has studied a carbon-rich asteroid. NASA's Galileo probe, bound for Jupiter, flew past the stony asteroids Gaspra in 1991 and Ida in 1993.
The NEAR spacecraft, travelling at 22,000 miles per hour, will snap more than 500 pictures as it soars 750 miles above the charcoal-black surface of Mathilde.
Scientists know very little about the space rock, which is about three times the size of New York City.

"I like to think of Mathilde as a stealth asteroid," said Donald Yeomans of the NEAR science team. "It's big. It reflects less than four percent of the light hitting it, making it coal black, probably one of the blackest objects in the solar system."
The probe's cameras will search for a possible "moonlet" orbiting the dark chunk of rock. A tiny moon might explain why the asteroid rotates slowly, making one complete turn every 17 days.
"We're hoping there might be some clues from the fly-by as to why Mathilde is rotating so slowly," said Yeomans.
The Galileo probe discovered a tiny moon, just one mile (1.6 km) across, orbiting around the asteroid Ida.
Scientists hope NEAR's close-up views will reveal features on Mathilde as small as a football field.
"One of the goals is to get the highest resolution pictures we can to just see what are the surface features on such an object," said Peter Thomas of the NEAR imaging team.
The first images from the spacecraft's high-speed pass will be made public on June 30, NASA officials said.
The NEAR spacecraft, which was launched from Cape Canaveral on Feb. 17, 1996, was developed at a cost of $122 million, making it one of NASA's cheapest deep space missions.
